Silver and gold own today’s tape. Copper owns the physical squeeze. Uranium owns the long-duration setup.

Hyundai bought control of Boston Dynamics at a $1.1B valuation in 2021. Today Unitree opened near $66B - 35x it's last VC round of $1.9B and ~7x its IPO price.

Unitree has real revenues and major brand presence, but the company is not very well understood by most investors. 

In 2025, it generated $131m in Humanoid sales. 70-80% of its Humanoid sales were for research use cases, 20-30% for education and entertainment, and very little for genuine robotic use cases. Unitree's main product was a robot body that lacked a brain.

An affordable, programmable, at least semi-reliable brainless humanoid body however, is exactly what the research market demanded. Unitree G1s are ubiquitous across robotics research groups around the world. Just as AI research is dependent on physical computing hardware, robot hardware is indispensable for research in robot learning, control systems, simulation, etc.

While there are few Unitree humanoids currently deployed for real robotic work, the rise of the company has greatly accelerated global research progress. It optimized for an axis (cheap dynamic locomotion) that allowed it to capture the research market but is different from the requirements of of the deployment market (intelligence, durability, payload, safety certification). However, a lot of the engineering capability they've built as a company can and is starting to be used to develop more deployment optimized hardware models.

This is a fundamentally different approach from most American humanoid companies which are building towards operational products for consumers and businesses in a straight shot. Companies like Figure and Apptronik invest more resources in R&D and don't yet offer it to retail because they want to go direct to the larger deployment markets. They are building towards a highly functional polished product that can eventually become a development platform like Apple (as opposed to starting as a development platform). For AI, Anthropic took the mass market product capital intensive approach and it took a lot of dollars and time before lifting off on revenue. Cohere and AI21 Labs have existed for a similar amount of time, and took a more capital-light path. AI21 had to pivot, while Cohere has continued to grow, although significantly more slowly than Anthropic. Neither approach is right or wrong and history is filled with examples of successful parallels for both. You cannot compare companies taking different approaches solely on a revenue multiple basis.

The company's commercial approach is a byproduct of the Chinese private capital markets. A market where there are not as many venture dollars as the US that are willing to fund hundreds of millions to billions for R&D before any revenue is generated. Revenue growth is required to fund the next rung of capital even for potentially massive TAMs. Actuator scaling parlayed into quadrupeds, quadrupeds into the dominant robot hardware research platform. This IPO funds their transition to the most ambitious phase yet - a company building vertically integrated intelligent robots across a wide variety of form factors.  

The current market valuation is suggesting that they will accomplish this transition, although it is not final yet. The outcome for Unitree differs dramatically based on if they can successfully move up market. Companies like DJI and Toyota have previously done so, while a failure to do so could have the company looking like Raspberry Pi. A company that cemented themselves within experimentalists and niche industrial markets.

However, it may not be necessary for Unitree to build SOTA research capabilities in order to scale robot sales into real deployments. If physical intelligence commoditizes, which we believe it does, then they could have plenty of externally produced models for their customers to choose from. The companies that can produce high quality hardware at scale stand to be large benefactors from the development of physical AGI.

The focus on hardware has enabled Unitree to raise a huge war chest and have access to thousands of robots that they can use for robot learning data collection and research. While various data types can be used in pretraining for robot foundation models, robot data is required for the models to become performant. To collect a large set of robot data, you will need a lot of robots. They may have actually created a stronger path for themselves to produce performant physical AI models than companies that have focused purely on robot model development years ago.

Wang Xingxing is famous for his technical chops, but he has also been an excellent business strategist.

It optimized for an axis (cheap dynamic locomotion) that allowed it to capture the research market but is different from the requirements of of the deployment market (intelligence, durability, payload, safety certification). However, a lot of the engineering capability they've built as a company can and is starting to be used to develop more deployment optimized hardware models.

This is a fundamentally different approach from most American humanoid companies which are building towards operational products for consumers and businesses in a straight shot. Companies like Figure and Apptronik invest more resources in R&D and don't yet offer it to retail because they want to go direct to the larger deployment markets. They are building towards a highly functional polished product that can eventually become a development platform like Apple (as opposed to starting as a development platform). For AI, Anthropic took the mass market product capital intensive approach and it took a lot of dollars and time before lifting off on revenue. Cohere and AI21 Labs have existed for a similar amount of time, and took a more capital-light path. AI21 had to pivot, while Cohere has continued to grow, although significantly more slowly than Anthropic. Neither approach is right or wrong and history is filled with examples of successful parallels for both. You cannot compare companies taking different approaches solely on a revenue multiple basis.

The company's commercial approach is a byproduct of the Chinese private capital markets. A market where there are not as many venture dollars as the US that are willing to fund hundreds of millions to billions for R&D before any revenue is generated. Revenue growth is required to fund the next rung of capital even for potentially massive TAMs. Actuator scaling parlayed into quadrupeds, quadrupeds into the dominant robot hardware research platform. This IPO funds their transition to the most ambitious phase yet - a company building vertically integrated intelligent robots across a wide variety of form factors.

The outcome for Unitree differs dramatically based on if they can successfully move up market. Companies like DJI and Toyota have previously done so, while a failure to do so could have the company looking like Raspberry Pi. A company that cemented themselves within experimentalists and niche industrial markets.

If physical intelligence commoditizes, which we believe it does, then they could have plenty of externally produced models for their customers to choose from. The companies that can produce high quality hardware at scale stand to be large benefactors from the development of physical AGI.

The focus on hardware has enabled Unitree to raise a huge war chest and have access to thousands of robots that they can use for robot learning data collection and research. While various data types can be used in pretraining for robot foundation models, robot data is required for the models to become performant. To collect a large set of robot data, you will need a lot of robots. They may have actually created a stronger path for themselves to produce performant physical AI models than companies that have focused purely on robot model development years ago.

Wang Xingxing is famous for his technical chops, but he has also been an excellent business strategist.

So, what happens when Bitcoin miners make more money from AI than mining Bitcoin?

A Bitcoin mining company just made 5x more money renting out compute than mining Bitcoin.

Almost every miner is going to announce a version of this pivot, and most of them won't be able to fund it.

For years Mining used to be simple. Whoever can turn electricity into $BTC cheapest gets to profit massively. 

But after the halving squeezed margins, many miners started asking a different question, 

“What else can we do with our power, land, cooling systems and data centers?”

Well A.I. exploded, and AI companies were hungry for resources.

So now Bitcoin mining companies like Core Scientific, IREN, Hut 8, TeraWulf, and others are converting mining infrastructure into AI/HPC data centers.

The numbers are already showing the shift.

Core Scientific generated around $136M from AI colocation compared to $27M from Bitcoin mining.

TeraWulf generated roughly 2.5x more revenue from HPC/AI hosting than crypto mining.

Meanwhile, neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Applied Digital are seeing massive demand for GPU compute.

For the simplest reason, Bitcoin mining created the perfect foundation for AI infrastructure.

- Cheap power.
- Large-scale facilities.
- Cooling expertise.
- High-density computing.

The same assets that once mined $BTC can now rent compute to AI companies.

But If miners can earn better returns selling compute than securing Bitcoin, what happens next for BTC?

Bitcoin mining isn’t disappearing, $BTC is still the core asset.

This transition alone isn't that easy. Building AI infrastructure is extremely expensive even if you have existing mining infrastructure.

TeraWulf estimates around $8M-$10M per critical MW to build these facilities. A 100MW site can require close to $1B in capital before generating any revenue.

The next evolution of Bitcoin mining might not be about mining more BTC. 

It might be about turning megawatts into long-term AI infrastructure contracts.

Not sure what happens long term but this is a trend that I find alarming. 

What do u think?

After a soft 20 yr auction on the heels of an eventful morning for the US Treasury, some further thoughts here on what has transpired. 
In my opinion, no lunch is free here. On one hand, we get lower long end rates (at least for today as I question the sustainability, just like with FX intervention) and Bessent is buying long term Treasuries well below par, likely those with coupons with a one handle or less that are trading at $.50 on the dollar and issued when short rates were at zero. But, by replacing that with T-bills currently yielding around 3.75%, US interest expense will go higher. Also, in response, the US dollar is trading at 3 month low today and if sustained, that imports inflation and could facilitate foreign selling of Treasuries for those not FX hedged.

Lastly, with even more short term bond issuance, it ties the hands (among other ties, like excessive gov’t spending) of Kevin Warsh & Co because raising short term rates (which I do not think will happen anytime soon) would be even more expensive for the US government, further inflate US debts and deficits, and result in another rise in long term rates. And, what happens if inflation flares up again, if Warsh doesn’t hike, the long end will do it for him.

What a box we are in.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗜 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮 3% 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻 $SNAP

I spent the last couple of days listening to many interviews with Evan Spiegel, trying to understand the company, its problems and, more importantly, where the opportunity might be.

The thesis is actually pretty simple.

$SNAP has around 971 million people using the platform every month and 493 million using it every day. Yet the entire company is currently valued at only around $9 billion.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗩𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗚𝗔𝗣

One way to understand how cheap that is is to look at how the market values each daily user:

$RDDT: approximately $241 per daily user
$META: approximately $393 per daily user
$SNAP: approximately $18 per daily user

Obviously, this comparison is not completely apples to apples. $META and $RDDT are much better at monetizing their users.

But that is exactly the point.

$SNAP does not need to become $META. It already has the users. It simply needs to become better at making money from them.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗨𝗦𝗜𝗡𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗔𝗟𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗬 𝗜𝗠𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗚

$SNAP reported its latest earnings on August 3, 2026.

Revenue grew 19% from a year earlier to $1.6 billion. Daily users grew 5%. Free cash flow increased from $24 million to $121 million, while the quarterly net loss fell from $263 million to $164 million.

The company is still losing money on an accounting basis, but the direction is clearly improving.

And when a company with almost 1 billion monthly users is valued at only around $9 billion, even relatively small improvements in monetization can have a huge effect on the value of the business.

𝗔𝗜 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗢𝗠𝗜𝗖𝗦

After listening to many interviews with Spiegel, it became pretty obvious to me that $SNAP could be one of the companies that benefits enormously from AI.

Historically, $SNAP has had to compete for attention and advertising dollars against giants such as $META and TikTok, while operating with a fraction of their resources.

AI changes some of that.

Engineering becomes cheaper. Advertising becomes more efficient. Recommendations improve. Content becomes more personalized. Smaller companies can do things that previously required much larger teams.

For $SNAP, that matters a lot.
They already have the users.
The problem has always been monetizing them.

If AI helps $SNAP close even a small part of the monetization gap between itself and the larger social platforms, the operating leverage could be enormous.

𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗚𝗟𝗔𝗦𝗦𝗘𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗕𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗔 𝗖𝗔𝗧𝗔𝗟𝗬𝗦𝗧

There is another interesting part of the story: Specs. $SNAP recently introduced its new augmented reality glasses at around $2,195.

I think there is a very good chance they will be a commercial flop. At that price, it is difficult to see them becoming a mass-market product.

Strangely, I think that could actually become a positive catalyst for the stock.

Spiegel has spent years pursuing augmented reality hardware. If Specs fail badly enough, perhaps management finally understands that this is not where the value of $SNAP is today and starts focusing more aggressively on the core business.

That would mean more attention on advertising, subscriptions, engagement, margins and monetizing the enormous user base they already have.

But $SNAP doesn’t need to close the entire gap. It doesn’t even need to come close.

It just needs to become less bad at monetizing the users it already has.

If that happens, I think this can easily be a 100% stock from here.

I initiated a 3% position today at $5.15 per share.
